metadata.title: Three You Can Take Back. One You Can't.
metadata.topic: CLAUDE BASICS · WHERE YOUR DATA GOES
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: where does one detail you type into an AI actually go, and which of those places can you walk back out of? Redo of the ai-explainer/hai-simple source — same four-level descent (conversation, product memory, provider systems, training) ranked by reversibility, re-voiced Feynman × MKBHD: explain the mechanism at each level (context window / on-account file / provider retention clock / probability-distribution nudge), name the design trade at each level (statelessness on purpose / memory-as-document / operability at the cost of instant undo / forward-only opt-out), land on the one door that opens once.

beats.narration_text: Someone types a sentence into an AI, then walks the word 'delete' back to 'undo.' That correction is the whole video. Your sentence goes to four places. Three of them let you walk back in. One of them is a door that opens once.

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('delete' -> 'undo') is visible on a late frame. BUG FOUND+FIXED: original triggerWords 'delete it' (two words) never matched because BrutalistHesitantWriter matches trigger words against single whitespace-split tokens (buildActs: core.toLowerCase() vs triggers list) — a multi-word trigger phrase can never equal a single token, so the correction silently never fired. Changed to single-word triggerWords 'delete' -> replacementWords 'undo', confirmed on frame pull.

beats.narration_text: Start with the sentence itself. Three facts: partner, hiking, near Denver. On their own, none of them tells you who you are. Together, they're a coordinate. Here's what's actually happening — three low-signal facts intersect, and the intersection is you, roughly, on a map.

Those three facts don't land in one place. They land in four, stacked, each narrower than the one above it. The narrowing is the whole design — each level keeps less of what you said, and keeps what it kept for longer. Volume down, permanence up.

Anthropic's education team laid these four out and I'm borrowing the taxonomy — it's correct. What they didn't draw is the axis that actually decides how careful you should be. Four places is the map. Reversibility is the compass.
Not where does it go. That's the wrong question. The right one: which of these can you walk back out of? Every level has a door. Three of them open both ways. One is a door that opens once.

Level one is the conversation itself. While the window is open, the model has your three facts in what's called the context window — a working memory that exists only for this exchange. Close the window and there's nothing to erase. It wasn't holding anything anywhere else. That's not a promise. That's the architecture.

Open a fresh chat tomorrow and it starts blank. Not discreet — empty. The model has no idea your partner hikes, and no route to that fact unless you retype it. Here's the trade they picked: statelessness, on purpose. You lose continuity; you gain that nothing carries over you didn't put there.

So the first door swings both ways. Close the tab; the detail is gone from the only place it was living. Level one is free — no request, no wait, no toggle. And here's the honest part: almost everything you ever type into an AI stops here. Level one is where the volume of your typing lives.
Level two is where the language gets loose. Products say things like 'the model remembers you.' That's marketing. Let's ask for the mechanism instead.

props.command: Show me what "the model remembers me" actually means — mechanically, step by step.
props.topic: CLAUDE BASICS · WHERE YOUR DATA GOES

beats.narration_text: Here's what that phrase hides. The model didn't remember you. A file on your account did — a small dossier of facts you or the product decided to save. That file gets read into the blank chat before you finish typing your first word. Same effect as memory. Very different machinery.

That distinction isn't pedantry — it is the whole point. A memory you can open is a memory you can edit. In most products you can read the file, change a line, clear it, or switch the whole feature off. This is a design choice: they made memory a document, not a black box. You get transparency; they get a feature they can honestly explain.

Second door still swings both ways — but somebody set the latch before you got here. Depending on the product, memory is on by default or waiting to be switched on. That default is a design decision; different companies made different calls. Either way it's a setting, and settings are checkable in about a minute.

Level three isn't the model at all. It's the provider's own machinery — the plumbing behind the chat window. That's four jobs stacked into one storage layer: keeping the service up, reviewing for abuse, fixing bugs, and internal research. Some companies add commercial uses. The mechanism is simple — the provider has a copy, in their systems, for their reasons.

Your three facts sit in that machinery for a retention period — days, weeks, or months depending on the provider. Here's the part worth saying plainly: that period is real, it's usually written down in a policy, and it isn't yours to set. The clock exists so their operations work. You are downstream of it.

Third door still opens both ways — past a clock you don't wind. You can file a deletion request. You cannot set the interval. That's the shape of the trade: they run a service, so they hold logs long enough to run it. You still have a lever; you just don't have the dial.
beats.note: Register upshift (Plain → Teardown): source's neutral 'You can ask for deletion. You don't set the interval.' expanded with the design-verdict framing 'a lever, not a dial' — the trade the provider optimized for (operability) explicitly named. Facts unchanged: you can request, you can't set the interval.

beats.narration_text: But notice what changed. This is the first level where 'being in control' stops meaning 'you can undo it,' and starts meaning 'you can file a request and wait.' The choice they optimized for is operability — running a real service — at the cost of your instant, unilateral undo. That's a real trade, not a broken one. But it is a trade.

Level four is training. Some providers use user conversations as raw material for the next model. Personal details are generally stripped out first through automated scrubbers — 'generally,' and that hedge belongs to them, not to me. Scrubbers are heuristics. Heuristics miss.

And then your sentence stops being a sentence. During training, tokens from your text nudge the model's probability distribution — the likelihood, for a given context, that one word follows another. Your three facts don't sit anywhere anymore. They become an adjustment. Not a record of you. A pattern.

manim.spec: The three detail tokens dissolve into a probability distribution over next-tokens. Words break to glyphs, glyphs settle into a bar distribution that nudges by a hair. No colour shift, no darkening — cream stage, warm ink, terracotta only on the single bar that moves. Reveal lands on the spoken word 'pattern'.

beats.narration_text: That's offered as reassurance — and it is one. Nobody can read your words back out; a pattern isn't a paragraph. It's also the door that doesn't swing. There is no procedure — technical or legal — to un-train a model on a conversation it has already absorbed. This is the one place where 'delete' has no meaning. Only 'don't next time.'

Where providers train on conversations, most let you opt out — and you should go find that toggle today, not later. But understand what it actually buys. It protects every conversation after you flip it. Not one before. The opt-out is forward-looking because the model itself is forward-looking. Yesterday's conversations are already inside yesterday's weights.
Four levels. Three doors that open both ways. One arch that doesn't.

That gives you a rule sharper than any blanket policy. Price what you share against the least reversible place it could reach — not the most likely one. Most of what you type never leaves level one. Decide as though it might. That's how you trade cheaply: budget for the worst case, not the median one, because reversibility is what you can't buy back later.
beats.note: Register upshift (Plain → Teardown): source's cautious 'gives you a rule to work from' promoted back to a design-verdict framing 'sharper than any blanket policy' — the closing clause 'reversibility is what you can't buy back later' names why worst-case pricing beats median-case pricing on this particular axis. Heuristic itself (facts + advice) unchanged.

beats.narration_text: And the cheapest habit on the list costs nothing. If the tool doesn't need the real name to do the job, don't give it the real name. Rewording an email works exactly as well with a placeholder in it. This is a genuine free trade — same output, less exposure. Design the input around what the model actually needs, not what feels natural to type.

Four places, and they are not the same kind of place. The conversation forgets when you close it — no state to carry. Memory is a file you can open and edit — a document, not the model. Provider systems hold your data on a clock you don't set — you have a lever, not a dial. Training turns your sentence into a pattern, and patterns don't un-learn. Opt-outs work forward only. Everything else is a setting you can go check in about five minutes.

props.artifactTitle: Three You Can Take Back. One You Can't.
artifactLines: 1 · the conversation — reversible. Close it and it's gone from the only place it lived. Statelessness, on purpose.
2 · product memory — reversible. Not the model remembering; a file on your account, re-read into every new chat.
3 · provider systems — partial. You can file a deletion request; you don't set the retention clock. Lever, not dial.
4 · training — not reversible. Your words become a probability nudge, and probability nudges don't un-learn.
opt-out protects every conversation after the toggle, and none before it — the model is forward-looking.
price what you share against the least reversible place it could reach, not the most likely one.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — read it with me. 'Walk me through the exact privacy and data settings for the AI tool I use most. Find four things: whether it keeps conversation history, whether it has a memory feature and whether it's on, the stated retention period on provider systems, and whether my conversations are used to train the next model. Then tell me which of those four I could reverse tomorrow, and which one I could not.' That last clause is the whole exercise — the first three answers will be toggles, and the fourth will be a date. Go deeper: which of those four settings would still bind you if the company got acquired tomorrow, and which travel with the account? Liam, in for Bear.
